props.title: Noroi: The Curse

sections.content: Noroi: The Curse (2005) revolutionized found footage horror by weaving an intricate supernatural mystery through fake documentary footage. Director Kōji Shiraishi crafted something far more complex than typical ghost hunting films like Grave Encounters (2011), creating a dense web of interconnected paranormal events that rewards careful viewing. The film's genius lies in how it builds dread through seemingly unrelated incidents - a psychic's TV appearance, mysterious deaths, and ancient rituals - that gradually reveal a terrifying bigger picture, similar to how Lake Mungo (2008) pieces together its tragedy through documentary elements.

sections.content: Noroi's influence on Asian horror mockumentaries can't be overstated. Films like Gonjiam: Haunted Asylum (2018) and The Medium (2021) followed its documentary-style framework but rarely matched its intricate plotting. Shiraishi's approach of treating supernatural horror with journalistic seriousness created a template for elevated found footage that values investigation over jump scares. The film's patient building of mythology through news clips, interviews, and archival footage established a new standard for documentary horror authenticity.

What sets Noroi apart is how it uses its format to explore Japanese folklore and urban legends. Unlike the straightforward hauntings of Ju-On: The Grudge (2002), Noroi delves deep into ancient curses, spirit possession, and psychic phenomena, presenting them through a modern investigative lens. This blend of traditional supernatural elements with contemporary documentary techniques influenced later works like One Cut of the Dead (2017), which similarly plays with format expectations. sections.content: After Noroi, Japanese horror increasingly embraced documentary-style storytelling. POV: A Cursed Film (2012) and Cult (2013) adopted similar investigative structures but focused more on immediate scares than Noroi's slow-burn mystery. The film's approach to building horror through research and investigation influenced international found footage, seen in films like The Taking of Deborah Logan (2014) and Hell House LLC (2015), which similarly use documentary frameworks to ground their supernatural elements.
